basis.text: No writer of 1863 gives a clock time for the charge; the reports bound it from about 17:00 and before dusk. The two stated readings are later: Oates (15th Alabama, 1878) puts the retreat from the 20th Maine's front 'just about sunset' (about 19:30) and the Maine commission's volume (1898) 'about 6:30 p. m.' (no source named). The default is the window between them.

default.label: About 18:30 to 19:30: no report of 1863 gives a clock time; two later readings, reasoned within the reports
default.basis_text: The two ends are the two stated readings, both of 1878 or later: about 6:30 p. m. (Maine volume of 1898, no source named) and just about sunset, about 19:30 (Oates, 1878, the officer opposite Chamberlain). The reports of 1863 do not contradict either: they allow the charge from about 17:00 and put 'nearly dark' and 'at dusk' after it. Every reading is an 'about'; the 20 minutes by which the two armies' clocks reportedly differed is not applied.

animation.note: The charge is drawn at 19:00, the midpoint of the window; not a documented time. The early floor 17:30 (the plan's value) and the first delegated window 16:00 to dusk stay selectable. Dusk and the advance on Round Top (Chamberlain 9 p.m.) follow the charge in the reports, so nothing in them forbids 19:00.

default.note: A window between the two later readings. It sits an hour or more later than the plan's 17:30, which the reports allow only as the earliest possible hour.

inference.step: No writer gives a clock reading for the charge. positions.label: About 19:30, just about sunset: Oates's account of 1878 of the retreat after the charge

inference.step: Oates, the officer opposite Chamberlain, wrote in 1878 that his regiment's retreat from the 20th Maine's front 'was just about sunset' and that the battle had begun 'four hours previously' (about 15:30 by his book of 1905). The retreat followed the charge and was the end of that fight, so the charge is read as at or a little before sunset (19:32); a memoir fifteen years after, hedged, and the retreat is the Confederate side's moment, not Chamberlain's order.

weighing.summary: No writer of 1863 gives a clock time for the charge. The reports bound it: the brigade was ordered into position about 4 p.m. (Rice, Welch), the Confederate attack on it began about 4:30 to 5 (Bane, Norton), Rice has above half an hour and Chamberlain an hour of struggle before the bayonet order, and 'nearly dark' (Barnes) and 'at dusk' (Chamberlain) come after it. That floor is about 17:00 to 17:30. Two later writers state an hour: the Maine volume of 1898, about 18:30 with no source named, and Oates (15th Alabama) in 1878, 'just about sunset' (19:32). Oates stood opposite Chamberlain, wrote 20 years earlier than the Maine volume and says how he counts (four hours after the battle began); the Maine volume names no basis. So the weight favours the later end, but a hedged memoir is not a clock reading: the window 18:30 to 19:30, class weighted (the evidence favours the later hours but does not settle them), tier inferred. The plan's 17:30 is the computed floor and is outweighed by both readings.
weighing.who: Rice, Chamberlain, Conner, Welch and Woodward wrote as officers of Vincent's brigade on the hill; none gives an hour for the charge. Bane (4th Texas) wrote for the Confederates against the brigade's centre. Barnes, the division commander, does not say he was at the ledge and relays the brigade's reports. Oates commanded the regiment that Chamberlain charged and wrote in 1878 and 1905. Norton, a private of the brigade, computes in 1913. The Maine and Pennsylvania volumes are state commission books with no named writer for the passages.
weighing.when: The reports are of 6 July to 24 August 1863, the best class of writing, but state lengths of time and starting hours, not an hour for the charge. Oates's 'just about sunset' is of 1878, 15 years after, a memoir of the second rank; the Maine volume is of 1898, 35 years after, also second rank, with no basis named. The earlier writing of a participant outranks the later unsourced narrative; the reports do not outrank either because they do not state the point. Woodward (6 July 1863) is the only writer of the time near an hour for the end of the fight ('nearly 6 p. m.'), but Norton shows his starting hours were wrong, so it is not used as a bound.
weighing.where: Chamberlain and Rice stood at the 20th Maine's position; Bane's Texans attacked the brigade's centre and right, so his 4:30 dates the first attack, which came before the flanking column reached the 20th Maine. Oates stood at the point of contact, so he saw the charge's effect: the retreat, which he dates by the sun. Barnes's 'nearly dark' and Chamberlain's 'At dusk' come after the charge.
weighing.how_knew: Oates dates by the sun ('just about sunset') and by four hours since the battle began; it is an estimate in a retrospective article. Chamberlain and Rice give lengths of time as estimates with the action in mind. The Maine volume and the monument inscription (brigade arrival about 5 p.m.) name no source. Norton computes.
weighing.clock: The Union reports use the Union clock, Bane and Oates the Confederate; the sun is the same for both: sunset 19:32. The reported difference of about 20 minutes between the armies' clocks is not applied. It is smaller than the hour between the window's ends and is uncertainty on every reading.
weighing.independence: Oates (1878), the Maine volume (1898) and the reports are three independent lines; the two stated hours are an hour apart and neither is a clock reading. The Maine volume's own account starts the action about 4 p.m. and does not say how its 6:30 was reckoned; if it counts a fight of two hours from the start, it would agree with a reading later than the computed floor. Oates 1905 is the same line as 1878 (his book repeats the account). The floor 17:30 rests on four lines (Rice, Chamberlain, Conner, Bane/Norton) but is a computation. Powell, Lossing and the Park Service texts follow the reports and give no hour.

source_panel_text: About 18:30 to 19:30 on Jul 2. No report of 1863 gives a clock time for the charge; they allow it from about 17:30. Two later writers do: a Maine volume of 1898 says about 6:30 p.m. (no source named), and Colonel Oates of the 15th Alabama wrote in 1878 that the retreat was just about sunset (19:32). The plan's 17:30 is the earliest possible hour. Five other values are listed.

what_would_change_it: A report, letter or diary of 1863 to 1864 with a clock reading for the order or for the repulse in front of the 20th Maine (a 20th Maine officer such as Spear, Morrill or Prince; Oates's or Law's letters; the battlefield commission or Bachelder papers) would replace the window. So would the Maine commission's source for 'about 6:30 p. m.', or the plan's key SS2 for 17:30. A second independent writer of the time for the sunset hour would make it settled.
owner_note: The first delegated default (about 17:30, window 16:00 to dusk) is replaced by a window 18:30 to 19:30 drawn at 19:00; nothing is deleted. 17:30 stays selectable as the floor the reports allow. If the owner wants a point instead, the candidates are 18:30 (Maine volume) and about 19:30 (Oates); neither is a clock reading of the day. The charge is not an arrival and is not read by the arrival gate.
